body.heading: A balanced beam on a tower
paragraphs: A tower crane is a giant balance. From the top of its mast, a horizontal jib reaches out over the building site, and a shorter counter-jib reaches the other way, carrying slabs of concrete counterweight. Load and counterweight pull against each other around the mast.

The balance is about turning force, not just weight: a load's tipping effect equals its weight multiplied by its distance from the mast. A modest load far out can tip as hard as a heavy load held close — the counterweights are sized to cover the worst case.

body.heading: Moving the load
paragraphs: A trolley rolls along the jib carrying the hook, so the driver can position the load at any radius; a winch winds the cable to raise and lower it. The whole top of the crane — jib, counter-jib and cab — rotates on a slewing ring to swing loads around the site.

Operators respect a load chart: the farther out the trolley, the less the crane may lift. Sensors measure the turning force continuously and cut power before the limit is passed, because a crane near its limit has no spare strength for gusts or swinging loads.

body.heading: Heavier than itself
paragraphs: The puzzle in this crane's job resolves like this: the structure does not lift the load by strength alone — the counterweights do half the work, and the mast channels the remaining forces down into a massive concrete base or the building itself.

A large tower crane can raise twenty tonnes or more, yet it arrives on site as a stack of flat-pack steel sections, assembled by a smaller mobile crane — and, as the building grows, it can climb with it, adding mast sections from within its own frame.

description: A tower crane lifts loads heavier than its own jib by balancing them against counterweights behind the mast.
